title: DID JESUS REALLY DECLARE ALL FOODS CLEAN? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE GOD, HOLINESS, AND GRACE
paragraphs: DID JESUS REALLY DECLARE ALL FOODS CLEAN? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE GOD, HOLINESS, AND GRACE

For centuries, Christians have wrestled with one uncomfortable question: If God once called certain foods unclean, why do millions of believers eat them today? Did God's standards change? Did Jesus abolish His Father's commandments? Or have we been missing something far greater than what is on our plates? The answer takes us from the holiness laws of ancient Israel to a rooftop vision, a divided dinner table, and the bloodstained cross where Jesus changed everything.
There is a question that can turn an ordinary Christian dinner into a theological battlefield.
Someone reaches for a piece of pork.
Another believer quietly shakes his head.
“You know the Bible says that's unclean, right?”
The first Christian smiles.
“But Jesus made all foods clean.”
Then comes the question neither of them expected.
“So was God wrong when He forbade it in the first place?”
Suddenly, nobody is talking about dinner anymore.
They're talking about the character of God.
The authority of Scripture.
The meaning of obedience.
And whether Christians have misunderstood something that God took seriously enough to put into His written Law.
Perhaps you've been there.
Maybe you grew up believing that eating pork, shrimp, or shellfish was sinful. Maybe someone warned you that Christians who eat those things are deliberately disobeying God.
Or perhaps you were taught that the Old Testament dietary laws no longer apply, but nobody ever explained why.
You simply heard, “We're under grace now.”
And somewhere inside, a question remained.
Does grace mean God stopped caring about holiness?
Before you answer, consider something that might challenge both sides of this debate.
The God who gave Leviticus 11 is the same God who sent Jesus Christ.
He did not become wiser.
He did not discover a mistake in His earlier commandments.
He did not change from a strict Father into a forgiving Son.
And Jesus did not come to rescue humanity from a Father whose laws were unreasonable.
The Father and the Son are united in holiness, truth, and love.
So if we want to understand whether Christians should follow the Old Testament dietary laws today, we cannot begin with our appetites, traditions, or denominational loyalties.
We must begin with Scripture.
And we must be willing to follow the truth even when it challenges what we've always believed.
Because the real question is not merely what a Christian is permitted to eat.
The deeper question is whether we understand what Jesus accomplished.
Travel back thousands of years.
Imagine standing among the Israelites after their deliverance from Egypt.
These were not ordinary circumstances.
They were a people whom God had rescued from slavery, brought into covenant with Himself, and called to live differently from the surrounding nations.
Their worship was different.
Their sacrifices were different.
Their calendar was different.
Even their meals were different.
In Leviticus 11, God identified animals that Israel could eat and animals that were to be regarded as unclean.
Land animals generally needed to both chew the cud and have divided hooves. Aquatic creatures needed fins and scales. Other categories of animals were addressed through additional distinctions.
The pig, for example, had a divided hoof but did not chew the cud.
Therefore, Israel was forbidden to eat it.
Leviticus 11:7–8 identifies the pig as unclean and commands Israel not to eat its flesh.
But notice something important.
God did not present these instructions as arbitrary culinary preferences.
He connected them to His holiness.
In Leviticus 11:44, the Hebrew text declares:
כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אָנִי
Ki ani Adonai Eloheikhem, vehitqaddishtem vihyitem qedoshim ki qadosh ani.
“For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy.” — Leviticus 11:44, KJV
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh) means holy, carrying the idea of being set apart.
And that changes how we understand the passage.
Israel's dietary laws were part of a larger covenant life in which God's people were taught to distinguish between holy and common, clean and unclean.
Even ordinary activities became reminders that they belonged to the LORD.
Their food was not merely food.
It was part of their covenant identity.
And we should never mock that.
We should never speak as though God's commandments were foolish or meaningless.
The Law was holy, righteous, and good, as Paul affirms in Romans 7:12.
But now comes the question that changes the entire conversation.
If these commandments were good, why don't most Christians observe them today?
To understand that, we must distinguish between God's unchanging holiness and the particular covenant obligations He gave to Israel.
Not every command God gave to a particular person or people was intended to function as an identical obligation for every believer in every era.
God commanded Noah to build an ark.
That command was righteous.
But faithfulness to God today does not require every Christian to construct a wooden vessel.
God commanded Israel to offer sacrifices through the priestly system.
Those commands were divinely given.
Yet Christians do not continue offering animals for the forgiveness of sins because Jesus Christ fulfilled what those sacrifices anticipated.
Hebrews 10 explains that the sacrifices under the Law pointed toward the once-for-all offering of Christ.
The issue is not whether God was right to command something.
The issue is how that command functions within the unfolding story of redemption.
And that story leads directly to Jesus.
Picture Him surrounded by religious leaders.
They are watching His disciples.
Not because the disciples have committed some spectacular crime.
But because they are eating with hands that have not undergone the customary ritual washing.
This is the setting of Mark 7.
The immediate controversy is not about someone eating pork.
It concerns ritual purity traditions and the accusation that Jesus' disciples were eating with defiled hands.
That distinction matters enormously.
Jesus confronts religious hypocrisy, exposing how human traditions can be elevated above God's commandments.
Then He teaches something that reaches deeper than the controversy itself.
In Mark 7:18–19, Jesus explains that what enters a person from outside does not enter the heart but the stomach and then passes out.
Mark adds a significant explanatory statement.
The Greek reads:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
Katharizōn panta ta brōmata.
Commonly understood in context as:
“Thus he declared all foods clean.” — Mark 7:19, ESV
The Greek word katharizōn comes from a verb meaning to cleanse or make clean.
The phrase panta ta brōmata means “all foods.”
This passage deserves careful handling.
The original Greek does not contain a separate verb meaning “declared” in this phrase. The ESV's wording expresses an interpretive understanding of Mark's grammatical construction.
Many modern translations understand Mark to be explaining the implications of Jesus' teaching: that all foods are clean.
Other interpreters understand the phrase differently, including as a reference to the digestive process.

And because Jesus' immediate dispute concerned ritual handwashing rather than a direct challenge about pork, Christians should acknowledge the contextual question instead of pretending there is no debate.
Nevertheless, Mark's Gospel presents a profound teaching about defilement.
Jesus redirects attention from external contamination to the moral corruption that proceeds from the human heart.
He says in Mark 7:21–23 that evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, envy, slander, pride, and foolishness come from within.
These things defile a person.
Read that again.
Jesus is not minimizing sin.
He is exposing its true depth.
A man can refuse every forbidden food and still destroy his marriage through adultery.
A woman can carefully observe dietary restrictions while secretly nurturing bitterness and hatred.
A religious leader can maintain an immaculate table while exploiting the poor.
Someone can spend years inspecting ingredients and never once seriously examine the cruelty coming out of their mouth.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal.
What good is a carefully guarded plate if the heart remains surrendered to sin?
Jesus is not teaching that outward obedience never matters.
He is teaching that external religious observance cannot substitute for a heart transformed by God.
And this is where the story begins to move beyond the dinner table.
Because there was another man who had spent his entire life honoring the dietary boundaries of Israel.
His name was Peter.
And one day, God interrupted everything he thought he understood.
Acts 10 tells us that Peter went onto a rooftop to pray.
He became hungry.
While food was being prepared, he fell into a trance and saw heaven opened.
Something like a large sheet descended, containing various kinds of animals.
Then came a command.
“Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” — Acts 10:13, KJV
Peter resisted.
“Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” — Acts 10:14, KJV
Imagine that moment.
Peter had walked with Jesus.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed the resurrection.
Yet he still regarded the eating of common or unclean things as unacceptable.
This detail reminds us that the early church's understanding of the implications of Christ's work developed as God revealed His purposes more fully.
Then the voice spoke again.
“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” — Acts 10:15, KJV
The event occurred three times.
But before anyone uses this passage as a quick answer to every dietary question, we must listen to Peter's own explanation.
Because Acts 10 is not primarily a story about Peter discovering a new menu.
It is about God breaking through a barrier between Jews and Gentiles.
The Holy Spirit was preparing Peter to enter the home of Cornelius, a Gentile.
In Acts 10:28, Peter explains the meaning he had come to understand:
“God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.” — KJV
There it is.
The vision's explicit application concerns people.
Gentiles were not to be treated as spiritually untouchable outsiders whom God could never welcome.
Through Jesus Christ, God was bringing the good news to the nations.
Peter later witnessed the Holy Spirit fall upon Gentile believers.
And the Jewish believers who accompanied him were astonished.
Why?
Because God's saving grace was reaching people they had not expected to receive it in this way.
The sheet was not merely a lesson about animals.
It was part of a revelation about the expanding family of God.
This means we should not claim that Acts 10, by itself, is a straightforward announcement abolishing every dietary restriction.
That goes beyond Peter's stated interpretation.
But neither should we ignore the wider New Testament teaching about food, covenant identity, and the inclusion of Gentiles.
And that brings us to a moment when the early church faced an explosive question.
Must Gentile believers come under the Law of Moses to belong fully to God's people?
The disagreement was so serious that the apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem.
Acts 15 records their deliberation.
Some argued that Gentile believers should be circumcised and commanded to keep the Law of Moses.
But Peter reminded the assembly that salvation comes through the grace of the Lord Jesus.
Then the church issued instructions to Gentile believers.
They were to abstain from things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, what had been strangled, and blood.
Notice what the apostles did not do.
They did not command Gentile converts to adopt the entire dietary system of Leviticus 11.
That omission is significant.
Yet we must also be accurate.

Acts 15 does not mean the apostles believed food-related conduct was entirely irrelevant. The instructions concerning blood, strangled animals, and idol-related food show that the church still addressed dietary practices in its communal life.
Christians differ on how those instructions apply today, particularly regarding their continuing force and their relationship to Jewish-Gentile fellowship.
But the central conclusion is unmistakable.
Gentile believers were not required to become Jewish proselytes and observe the whole Mosaic Law in order to be saved or accepted as God's people.
Salvation was not obtained through a change of diet.
It was received through the grace of Jesus Christ.
And Paul would later make this truth even clearer.
In Romans 14, he addresses believers who differ over food and special days.
Some eat freely.
Others abstain because of conscience.
Paul does not tell the stronger believer to mock the weaker.
He does not tell the abstaining believer to condemn the one who eats.
Instead, he calls both to honor the Lord.
Romans 14:3 says:
“Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him.” — KJV
That last phrase is extraordinary.
For God hath received him.
Not because his plate satisfied the judgment of every Christian around him.
Not because he successfully defended his position in a theological argument.
But because he belonged to the Lord.
Romans 14:14 records Paul's conviction that nothing is unclean in itself, while recognizing that a person who regards something as unclean must take that conscience seriously.
Romans 14:20 likewise says that all things are indeed pure, while warning against using food in a way that causes another believer to stumble.
The passage is not permission to disregard conscience.
It is a call to let love govern liberty.
And in Romans 14:17, Paul gives us a sentence that deserves to be written across every Christian argument about food:
“For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.” — KJV
Think about how much unnecessary pain might have been avoided if Christians had remembered that.
Families divided over food.
Believers accusing one another of rebellion.
New converts frightened into thinking they could lose God's acceptance through an unfamiliar meal.
Others arrogantly ridiculing Christians whose consciences remain sensitive about what they eat.
And all the while, Scripture is calling us to something higher.
Righteousness.
Peace.
Joy in the Holy Spirit.
The same apostle writes in Colossians 2:16–17:
Paul's language of shadow and substance points us toward the fulfillment found in Christ.
This does not make the Old Testament worthless.
Quite the opposite.
A shadow can reveal something about the reality toward which it points.
But when the reality arrives, we must not confuse the shadow with the Savior.
The Law reveals God's holiness.
The sacrificial system anticipates redemption.
Israel's covenant distinctions help us understand the extraordinary significance of God bringing the nations together in Christ.
And Jesus stands at the center of the entire story.
He said in Matthew 5:17:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.” — KJV
That word fulfil matters.
The Greek verb is πληρόω (plēroō), which can mean to fill, complete, or bring to fulfillment.
Jesus did not come to treat the Scriptures as meaningless.
He came to bring God's redemptive purposes to their intended fulfillment.
And the New Testament explains that Christ's work establishes a new covenant.
Hebrews 8:13 speaks of the first covenant becoming obsolete in light of the new.
Ephesians 2:14–16 describes Christ breaking down the dividing wall of hostility and creating one new humanity through His cross.
The question, therefore, is not whether Christians should despise the Law.
Never.
The question is whether the Mosaic covenant's dietary restrictions remain binding requirements for Christians living under the new covenant.

The mainstream Christian understanding, supported by Mark 7, Acts 15, Romans 14, Colossians 2, and the New Testament's teaching about the new covenant, is that Christians are not required to observe the clean-and-unclean animal distinctions of Leviticus 11.
That conclusion does not mean every Christian tradition agrees.

Some Seventh-day Adventists, Messianic Jewish believers, and other Torah-observant Christians continue to abstain from foods classified as unclean in Leviticus 11, though their theological reasons and interpretations differ.
Some understand the distinctions as continuing divine instructions.
Others emphasize health, identity, tradition, or conscience.
Their convictions should be represented fairly.
And Christians who disagree should still treat one another with dignity.
But no Christian should confuse dietary observance with the saving work of Jesus Christ.
We are not justified by what we eat or refuse to eat.
We are justified through faith in Christ, not through works of the Law, as Paul teaches in Galatians 2:16.
And now, perhaps, we are ready to answer the question that brought us here.
Should Christians follow the Old Testament dietary laws today?
Christians may choose to observe those dietary restrictions as a matter of conscience, personal discipline, cultural practice, or religious conviction.
But under the New Testament's teaching about Christ and the new covenant, observance of Leviticus 11 is not a universal requirement for Christian salvation or holiness.
A Christian who abstains from pork out of sincere conviction should not be mocked.
A Christian who eats pork with thanksgiving to God should not automatically be condemned as disobedient.
Both are accountable to Christ.
Both must act in faith.
Both must love their neighbors.
And neither may use food as a substitute for the righteousness that comes through Jesus.
There are, of course, other legitimate reasons to avoid particular foods.
Medical conditions.
Allergies.
Health concerns.
Personal discipline.
Cultural sensitivities.
Concern for another believer's conscience.
Christian freedom is not a command to eat everything.
Nor is it permission to act selfishly.
Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.” — KJV
And that is where the matter becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us have spent years asking whether our food is acceptable to God while avoiding questions about our conduct.
We want to know whether shrimp is forbidden.
But are we willing to confront the gossip we spread?
We debate whether pork is unclean.
But what about the pornography we keep returning to?
We inspect the ingredients of our meals.
But when was the last time we inspected the bitterness we carry toward someone who hurt us?
We argue over religious traditions.
But do we forgive?
Do we tell the truth when lying would benefit us?
Do we love people who cannot repay us?
Do we care about the poor?
Do we repent when the Holy Spirit convicts us?
These questions do not make dietary convictions meaningless.
They expose the danger of using external observance to hide internal rebellion.
And Jesus knows the difference.
He knows when obedience comes from love.
He knows when religion becomes a performance.
He knows when we are more interested in winning an argument than surrendering our hearts.
And He knows the sins we have managed to conceal behind a respectable Christian appearance.
Maybe that's the uncomfortable part of this article.
You came expecting an answer about food.
But Scripture has brought you face-to-face with your own heart.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer whether you should eat something.
Perhaps it is whether you have truly surrendered everything to Christ.
Because the tragedy of religious pride is that it can make us feel clean while leaving us spiritually empty.
You can know Hebrew.
You can quote Greek.
You can defend your doctrine.
You can avoid every forbidden ingredient.
And still desperately need the mercy of Jesus.
So can the Christian who proudly celebrates freedom while secretly living in sin.
Both need the same Savior.
Both need the same cross.
Both need the same grace.
And this is why the Gospel is so much greater than a religious food debate.
We were not saved because we finally learned the correct dietary interpretation.
We were saved because the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The cross did not make sin acceptable.
It revealed how serious sin truly is.
And the resurrection declared that death would not have the final word.
Through repentance and faith in Christ, guilty people can receive forgiveness.
The spiritually dead can receive new life.
The ashamed can find mercy.
The rebellious can be reconciled to God.
The outsider can be welcomed into God's family.
And the person who has spent years trying to earn divine acceptance can finally discover that salvation is God's gift of grace.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
But don't stop at verse 9.
Verse 10 reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us unchanged.
It transforms the way we live.
It teaches us to reject ungodliness.
It moves us toward holiness.
It produces gratitude, obedience, humility, generosity, and love.
We do not obey to purchase salvation.
We obey because the Savior who purchased our redemption is worthy of our lives.
And that includes what we do at the dinner table.
Eat with gratitude.
Abstain with a clear conscience.
Do not weaponize your freedom.
Do not worship your restrictions.
Do not destroy fellowship over a meal.
And never forget the One who gave His life so that sinners could be brought near to God.
There is something beautiful about the picture Scripture gives us of God's redeemed people.
In Revelation 7:9, John sees a multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne and before the Lamb.
Different histories.
Different cultures.
Different earthly customs.
But one Redeemer.
One salvation.
One Lamb who was slain.
Imagine that.
People who once would never have shared a table are united in worship because of Jesus Christ.
Not because every cultural distinction disappeared.
Not because every believer had identical personal convictions.
But because the blood of Jesus accomplished what human effort never could.
Reconciliation.
Redemption.
A new people belonging to God.
And perhaps that is the truth we most desperately need to recover.
The Christian faith is not ultimately about building a life that looks religious enough to impress God.
It is about being reconciled to Him through His Son and learning to live as people who have been redeemed.
Maybe you have been judging someone because of what they eat.
Repent of that pride.
Maybe you have mocked someone who abstains because of sincere conviction.
Repent of that arrogance.
Maybe you have been using grace as an excuse to ignore the clear moral commands of Scripture.
Repent of that compromise.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove your righteousness through religious performance because deep down you are terrified that God will reject you.
Hear the invitation of Jesus.
Come to Him.
Not with a perfect record.
Not with a carefully constructed image.
Not with a list of religious achievements.
Come with repentance and faith.
Come confessing your need.
Come trusting the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the heart of Christianity is not that you managed to make yourself clean enough for God.
It is that Jesus Christ is able to cleanse sinners and make them new.
And when He changes a life, holiness is no longer merely a collection of external rules.
It becomes the fruit of belonging to Him.
If this truth has challenged you, don't rush away from the conviction.
Sit with it.
Pray over it.
Open your Bible and examine the passages for yourself.
Ask the Holy Spirit to expose anything in your heart that needs to change.
Or share what Scripture has taught you about Christian freedom, conscience, and holiness. You may disagree with parts of this article, and thoughtful, Scripture-grounded discussion is welcome.
You don't have to pretend you've figured everything out.
Sometimes spiritual growth begins with the humility to say, “Lord, teach me.”
Because Christian discipleship should never stop at discovering the right answer.
It should lead us to worship, repentance, love, and transformation.
That is also why we are building something beyond a single article.
We want people who cannot afford expensive Christian resources to have opportunities to study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and grow in biblical understanding.
And we want this ministry to keep reaching more people.
That takes time.
It takes work.
It takes resources.
And it takes believers who understand that spreading the Gospel is a shared mission.

Some believers choose to support ministries as part of their regular Christian giving. If you regard this support as an offering, give freely and prayerfully, according to your convictions and circumstances.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that God loves a cheerful giver, not one who gives under compulsion.
And that is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through fear.
Not through guilt.
But because you may genuinely desire to help more people hear His Word.
These products are simply an additional expression of gratitude. The greater purpose is to support ongoing biblical teaching and discipleship.
A thoughtful comment may encourage a believer who feels alone in their questions.
A simple tag may lead a friend back to Scripture.
And a prayer offered in secret is never insignificant before God.
There is room in this mission for people who can give financially and for those who cannot.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is not a product.
We simply want to keep pointing people toward the Savior who freely gives what money could never buy.
Before you leave, remember how this entire journey began.
With a plate of food.
A disagreement.
A question about holiness.
But look where Scripture has brought us.
To the God who called Israel to be holy.
To the Savior who exposed the corruption of the human heart.
To Peter's rooftop, where God taught him not to call people unclean whom He was welcoming.
To the early church, where Gentile believers were received through grace rather than required to adopt the entire Mosaic Law.
To the cross, where Jesus gave Himself for our redemption.
And to a future where people from every nation will worship the Lamb together.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
It does not trivialize God's holiness.
It reveals how sinners can be made holy through Christ.
It does not teach us to despise obedience.
It teaches us to obey from a heart transformed by grace.
It does not make food the measure of our righteousness.
It points us to Jesus, who alone is our righteousness and our hope.
So the next time someone asks you whether Christians should follow the Old Testament dietary laws, don't merely give them a slogan.
Open the Scriptures.
Explain the covenants.
Honor the context.
Acknowledge sincere differences.
Speak the truth in love.
And above all, lead them to Jesus.
Because the greatest scandal was never that someone ate what another person considered unclean.
The greatest scandal is that holy God would show such astonishing mercy to guilty sinners through the sacrifice of His beloved Son.
And the greatest grace is that those sinners can be forgiven, restored, and transformed through faith in Him.
The meal on your table cannot wash away your sins—but the Savior who gave Himself on the cross can make your heart new.
